query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges under extreme service conditions when high strain rates and/or very low temperatures induce localized grain boundary decohesion through dynamic cavitation and/or local amorphization, rather than through conventional grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., a CoCrFeMnNi-type alloy) prepared with minimal grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to systematically varied mechanical loading conditions (quasi‐static versus high strain rate) and temperature regimes (room temperature versus cryogenic/low temperature) while keeping alloy composition and processing constant.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant boundaries including regimes of high strain rate impact or cyclic loading at low temperatures, as compared to baseline quasi-static loading at moderate temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary decohesion mediated by the formation of nanocavities and/or localized amorphous intergranular regions during high stress concentration events.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain rate or low-temperature loading, the uniform matrix cannot redistribute local stresses effectively; the resultant concentration of stresses at grain boundaries leads to dynamic cavitation (and possibly amorphization) at these boundaries. This process reduces the cooperative plastic deformation capability even in the absence of compositional segregation or intermetallic precipitation, thereby transitioning the alloy from ductile to brittle failure modes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to quasi-static, room-temperature tests (baseline), samples loaded at high strain rates or at cryogenic temperatures will exhibit a measurable reduction in fracture toughness, with microscopic evidence (via TEM or high-resolution microscopy) of cavitation or amorphous intergranular films at grain boundaries. This behavior contrasts with conventional alloys, where brittleness is typically preceded by compositional segregation or brittle precipitate formation.
generation.baseline: The initial homogeneous, single-phase HEA under moderate loading and temperature conditions, showing high toughness and ductility with no grain boundary cavitation or amorphous film formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is intended to apply within engineering service conditions that are extreme (e.g., high strain rate impact or low temperature) but still within the operational limits of the alloy; results outside these regimes may involve additional mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold levels of strain rate and temperature at which the transition occurs, as well as the sensitivity of the cavitation/amorphization process to minor compositional variations and stress state details, remain uncertain and require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical samples of a single-phase high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to quasi-static loading at room temperature (baseline) and the other to high strain rate loading at cryogenic temperatures. Conduct in-situ high-resolution electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) to monitor grain boundary behavior during deformation, and perform fracture toughness measurements post-test.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) of grain boundaries for evidence of cavitation or local amorphization
Strain rate and temperature profile verification during testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain rate/low temperature samples do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in toughness and lack clear microscopic evidence of grain boundary cavitation or amorphous intergranular films relative to the baseline, the hypothesis that brittle behavior is induced by a dynamic decohesion mechanism rather than conventional segregation/precipitation is falsified.

Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution. frame.system: Compositionally complex, initially single-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that maintain a homogeneous microstructure without conventional grain-boundary segregations or intermetallic precipitates.
frame.goal: To develop a testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the emergence of brittle behavior (loss of toughness) in these HEAs and to determine under what conditions this degradation occurs.
frame.limitation: Existing findings do not establish the governing factors behind toughness degradation in initially single-phase HEAs despite their resistance to conventional mechanisms like grain-boundary segregation and precipitation dominant in conventional alloys.
root_cause_cues: grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation
suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation
constraints: Alloy must remain compositionally complex and suitable for demanding engineering service
Retain a single-phase microstructure as the baseline state
frame.regime: Testing under service-relevant conditions that may include high-temperature exposure (to assess softening) and low-temperature conditions (to assess embrittlement) along with controlled mechanical loading (both quasi-static and dynamic) to map out the transition from ductile to brittle behavior.
prior_attempts: Conventional alloys were studied by attributing toughness degradation to grain-boundary segregation and precipitation phenomena; however, these models do not account for the observed robustness of HEAs against those conventional degradation mechanisms.

families.principle: Isolating the effect of individual processing or environmental parameters on the mechanical behavior to directly test the hypothesis.
cues_for: predicted observations relative to the initial baseline
cues_against: The question does not emphasize microstructure measurement techniques as the sole path
families.best_lever: Design an experiment comparing HEA samples subjected to systematic variations in temperature and mechanical loading (e.g., varying strain rates or cyclic loading) while maintaining the single‐phase, complex composition, to see if a transition to brittle behavior correlates with a threshold parameter.

families.principle: Integrating controlled experimental data with atomistic or mesoscale simulations for comprehensive validation of the mechanistic hypothesis.
cues_against: The need to keep a compositionally complex and single-phase baseline may limit overly complex simulation models if not tightly coupled with experiments
families.best_lever: Implement a combined approach where controlled variable experiments (e.g., varying temperature and load) are performed and the resultant mechanical response and microstructural changes are directly compared with simulation predictions. This coupling would decisively falsify the hypothesis if simulations and experiments do not converge on the same activation of brittleness mechanisms.

families.principle: Monitoring microstructural evolution and local deformation mechanisms in real time to detect incipient changes that may lead to embrittlement.
cues_for: suppression of conventional segregation and precipitate formation
cues_against: The question stresses a controlled comparison rather than using observational characterization alone
families.best_lever: Employ advanced techniques (such as in situ high-resolution electron microscopy or synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction) during mechanical testing to detect subtle changes (e.g., local strain localization or nanoscale phase evolution) that could serve as early indicators of brittleness.

families.principle: Using computational models to resolve the atomic and mesoscale origins of embrittlement, linking stress/strain fields to potential microstructural changes.
cues_for: explain whether and why brittle behavior emerges
cues_against: The question calls for a controlled experimental comparison and testable hypothesis in a real system rather than a simulation-only approach
families.best_lever: Develop a simulation that mimics the homogeneous single‐phase composition and applies different loading conditions, thereby testing if local atomic rearrangements or clustering phenomena (absent in conventional alloys) are responsible for the brittle transition.
